summary: Nevada treats an e-bike as a bicycle, not a motor vehicle. No licence, no registration, no plate. What the law does control is where you ride and what your bike has on it.

rules.text: You can ride an e-bike anywhere a regular bicycle is allowed: streets, roads, bike lanes, bike paths and shared-use paths.

There are three classes. Class 1 and class 2 stop assisting at 20 mph; class 3 stops at 28 mph. The motor cannot be more than 750 watts, and the bike must have working pedals and a seat. A moped or an electric scooter is not an e-bike.
On the road you have the same rights and the same duties as someone driving a car. Stop signs, red lights and signalling all apply to you.

At night your bike needs a white front lamp visible 500 feet ahead, a red rear reflector, and reflective material or a lamp visible from both sides. It also needs a brake good enough to skid the wheel on dry pavement.
The motor has to cut out when you stop pedalling or squeeze the brakes, a class 3 bike must have a speedometer, and you cannot modify the bike to go faster without replacing the class label.

No state law makes you wear a helmet on an e-bike. Nevada's headgear rule covers motorcycles and mopeds, and an electric bicycle is legally neither. Your city or county can still have its own rule, so check locally.

displayName: Riding a dirt bike, quad or side-by-side
summary: The opposite of an e-bike. An off-highway vehicle has to be titled and registered with the DMV, and putting one on a public road is tightly limited.

rules.text: If you own an OHV bought on or after July 1, 2011, you have 30 days from getting it to apply to the DMV for a certificate of title and registration.
You can ride on public land, trails, ways and unpaved county roads unless the agency in charge of that land has closed it to off-highway vehicles.

You cannot ride on a paved road that is not marked for OHV use. You can cross one if you come to a complete stop first and cross close to a right angle, and you can move it far enough to load or unload it.

To ride on a highway at all you need a valid driver's licence. Never on an interstate, never more than 2 miles along a paved highway, and in a city of 100,000 or more only on roads specifically designated for OHVs.
rules.appliesIf: You are on a highway rather than a trail or public land.

rules.text: On a highway you must wear a helmet, obey every traffic law, and have the registration attached to the vehicle.
rules.appliesIf: You are on a highway rather than a trail or public land.

displayName: Getting a permit and a licence
summary: Nevada runs a graduated system. Permit at 15 and a half, licence at 16 with 50 logged hours behind it, then a night curfew until you turn 18.

rules.text: You can apply for an instruction permit once you are 15 and a half. You have to pass every part of the exam except the driving test.

With a permit you can only drive when a licensed driver who is at least 21, and has at least a year of driving experience, is sitting in the seat beside you. The permit lasts one year and does not cover motorcycles.

For a licence at 16 or 17 you need driver education, 50 hours of supervised driving with at least 10 of them after dark, a log signed by your parent or guardian, and proof you are enrolled in school or have finished.
You also have to have held the permit for at least 6 months, and to have had no at-fault crash and no moving violation or alcohol or drug conviction in the 6 months before you apply.

Once licensed at 16 or 17 you cannot drive between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. unless you are going to or from a scheduled event. An officer cannot pull you over just to check this; it only comes up if you were already stopped for something else.
rules.appliesIf: You hold a licence issued at 16 or 17.

displayName: Taking a boat or jet ski out
summary: The rule that catches people out is boater education. If you were born on or after January 1, 1983, you need a safety card for anything over 15 horsepower on Lake Mead or Lake Tahoe.

rules.text: If you were born on or after January 1, 1983, you cannot operate a power-driven vessel with a motor over 15 horsepower on the state's interstate waters unless you have passed an approved boating safety course and hold the certificate for it.
rules.appliesIf: You were born on or after January 1, 1983, and the motor is over 15 horsepower.

rules.text: If a game warden or officer stops you, you have to show the certificate, a Coast Guard licence, a temporary permit, or a rental agreement naming you as an authorised operator.

The requirement is written for the "interstate waters of this State", and chapter 488 never defines that phrase. Lake Mead is shared with Arizona and Lake Tahoe with California, so both are normally treated as interstate waters. A lake sitting entirely inside Nevada may not be. Check before you rely on this.
You have to be at least 14 to operate a personal watercraft such as a jet ski, and everyone aboard has to wear a Coast Guard approved life jacket.
rules.appliesIf: You are on a personal watercraft rather than a boat.

rules.text: Anyone under 13 on a boat has to wear a Coast Guard approved life jacket the whole time the boat is under way, unless they are below deck or inside an enclosed cabin.
